import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import RocCurveDisplay, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

SEED = 43206
PREDICTORS = ["mean_radius", "mean_texture", "mean_smoothness"]

Question 1: Compare KNN and logistic regression

Use breast-cancer.csv, which contains 569 cases from the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset. Predict y (1 for malignant and 0 for benign) using mean_radius, mean_texture, and mean_smoothness.

Set a random seed and randomly split the observations into 70% training and 30% test data. Use the same split for every model. Standardize the predictors using the training means and standard deviations, and apply the same transformations to the test data.

Fit ordinary logistic regression with an intercept and no penalty, and KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{5,15,25,35,45}. k\in\{5,15,25,35,45\}.

Using the estimated probabilities for y = 1 on the test data, plot all six ROC curves in one figure and report their AUC values. Which of the six fitted models do you prefer? Give a brief justification based on your results.

Answer

I used a stratified random split so that the malignant/benign proportions were similar in the training and test sets. The scaler was fitted only on the training predictors and then applied unchanged to the test predictors.

cancer = pd.read_csv("data/breast-cancer.csv")
X = cancer[PREDICTORS]
y = cancer["y"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.30,
    random_state=SEED,
    stratify=y,
)

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_std = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_std = scaler.transform(X_test)

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "sample": ["Training", "Test"],
        "n": [len(y_train), len(y_test)],
        "benign (y=0)": [(y_train == 0).sum(), (y_test == 0).sum()],
        "malignant (y=1)": [(y_train == 1).sum(), (y_test == 1).sum()],
    }
)
sample n benign (y=0) malignant (y=1)
0 Training 398 250 148
1 Test 171 107 64

I fitted ordinary logistic regression with an unpenalized intercept. For every KNN model, I used Euclidean distance and uniform neighbor weights.

q1_models = {
    "Logistic regression": LogisticRegression(
        penalty=None,
        solver="lbfgs",
        max_iter=10_000,
    ),
    **{
        f"KNN, k={k}": KNeighborsClassifier(
            n_neighbors=k,
            weights="uniform",
            metric="euclidean",
        )
        for k in [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]
    },
}

q1_rows = []
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))

for model_name, model in q1_models.items():
    model.fit(X_train_std, y_train)
    test_probability = model.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]
    test_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probability)
    q1_rows.append({"Model": model_name, "Test AUC": test_auc})
    RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(
        y_test,
        test_probability,
        name=f"{model_name} (AUC={test_auc:.3f})",
        ax=ax,
    )

ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", linewidth=1, label="Chance")
ax.set_title("Test ROC curves")
ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
plt.show()

q1_auc = pd.DataFrame(q1_rows).sort_values("Test AUC", ascending=False)
q1_auc.style.format({"Test AUC": "{:.4f}"}).hide(axis="index")
Model Test AUC
KNN, k=45 0.9855
KNN, k=35 0.9847
Logistic regression 0.9829
KNN, k=15 0.9767
KNN, k=25 0.9725
KNN, k=5 0.9673

I prefer KNN with k=45k=45 because it has the largest test AUC, 0.9855, among the six fitted models for this fixed split. KNN with k=35k=35 is a close second (AUC 0.9847), and logistic regression ranks third (AUC 0.9829). The observed differences are small; this preference is based specifically on the requested test-set AUC rather than evidence that k=45k=45 will always be best on another random split.

Question 2: Training and test ROC curves

Use the same data, training/test split, and standardization as in Question 1. Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{1,3,5,10,20}. k\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}.

Use each fitted model to estimate probabilities for both the training and test observations. For training predictions, include each observation itself among its kk nearest neighbors.

For each kk, use a separate panel to show the training and test ROC curves together. Report both AUC values.

Explain the difference between training and test performance and how it changes with kk. In particular, explain what happens at k=1k=1 and why training performance may not reflect performance on new observations.

Answer

The code below uses exactly the same split and standardized predictors as in Question 1. Calling predict_proba on the training matrix includes each training observation itself among its nearest neighbors, as required.

q2_k_values = [1, 3, 5, 10, 20]
q2_rows = []

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 7))
axes = axes.ravel()

for ax, k in zip(axes, q2_k_values):
    model = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k,
        weights="uniform",
        metric="euclidean",
    )
    model.fit(X_train_std, y_train)

    train_probability = model.predict_proba(X_train_std)[:, 1]
    test_probability = model.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]
    train_auc = roc_auc_score(y_train, train_probability)
    test_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, test_probability)

    q2_rows.append(
        {"k": k, "Training AUC": train_auc, "Test AUC": test_auc}
    )

    RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(
        y_train,
        train_probability,
        name=f"Training (AUC={train_auc:.3f})",
        ax=ax,
    )
    RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(
        y_test,
        test_probability,
        name=f"Test (AUC={test_auc:.3f})",
        ax=ax,
    )
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", linewidth=1)
    ax.set_title(f"k = {k}")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
    ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)

axes[-1].axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

q2_auc = pd.DataFrame(q2_rows)
q2_auc.style.format(
    {"Training AUC": "{:.3f}", "Test AUC": "{:.3f}"}
).hide(axis="index")
k Training AUC Test AUC
1 1.000 0.892
3 0.991 0.949
5 0.982 0.967
10 0.979 0.978
20 0.978 0.974

At k=1k=1, every training observation is its own nearest neighbor. Its estimated probability is therefore exactly its observed class (0 or 1), producing a training AUC of 1.000. This is memorization rather than convincing evidence of generalization: the corresponding test AUC is only 0.892 because a new case cannot use itself as a neighbor.

Increasing kk smooths the fitted probabilities by averaging over more nearby observations. The training AUC consequently decreases from 1.000 at k=1k=1 to about 0.978 at k=20k=20, while the test AUC initially improves, reaching 0.978 at k=10k=10, and then slips slightly to 0.974 at k=20k=20. Thus, very small kk has low training error but high variance and overfits this training sample. Moderate kk generalizes better here. If kk becomes too large, averaging over a broad neighborhood can oversmooth genuine class structure, which explains why test performance need not keep improving. More generally, training performance is optimistic because it evaluates a model on the same observations used to fit it; performance on held-out observations is the relevant check for prediction on new cases.

Assignment Issue: Homework 6 peer grading assignment

Assigned reports:

  • c-schwarzbach, Homework 5

1. Report, question, and specific item for improvement:

I selected c-schwarzbach’s Homework 5 report, Question 4. The display code for the three misclassified handwritten digits fixes the image scale at vmin=0 and vmax=1. The ZIP digit data contain negative pixel values, so this scale clips every negative value to the same endpoint and removes visible intensity differences. The plot should use the full pixel range so that the displayed digits faithfully represent the observations used by the classifier.

2. Exact quotation and your own assessment (no AI assistance):

The relevant plotting code is:

plt.imshow(
    zip_test[i, 1:].reshape(16, 16),
    cmap="gray_r",
    vmin=0,
    vmax=1,
    interpolation="nearest",
)

The ZIP digit predictors use normalized grayscale values that include negative values, but the displayed images are restricted to the range from 0 to 1. Matplotlib clips values below vmin to the lowest displayed color, so all negative pixel intensities are rendered identically. This removes intensity differences that are present in the observations used by the KNN classifier. Because the discussion tries to explain why particular digits were misclassified from their appearance, the clipped plots provide less visual evidence than the underlying data contain. The classification calculations and reported error rates are unaffected; the issue is limited to how the example images are displayed.

3. Corrected or improved answer:

The KNN predictions and error rates do not need to be recomputed because the problem occurs only in the visualization. I would plot the same three misclassified observations using the full intensity range of the ZIP images. A fixed common scale keeps the panels comparable while preserving the negative pixel values:

incorrect = np.flatnonzero(euclidean_pred != y_test)[:3]

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3))
for j, i in enumerate(incorrect):
    plt.subplot(1, 3, j + 1)
    plt.imshow(
        zip_test[i, 1:].reshape(16, 16),
        cmap="gray_r",
        vmin=-1,
        vmax=1,
        interpolation="nearest",
    )
    plt.title(
        f"True: {y_test[i]}   Predicted: {euclidean_pred[i]}"
    )
    plt.axis("off")

plt.tight_layout()

This revision changes only how the images are displayed. It preserves the original observations, Euclidean-distance calculations, 5NN predictions, and reported test error, while showing the full grayscale information needed to understand the classification mistakes.
